title: Deployment DevOps And Production Infrastructure
description: Formalize deployment itself into genuine production infrastructure: extending Module 21's test-only CI/CD pipeline into a complete build-and-deploy pipeline, containerizing applications with Docker for genuinely consistent environments, managing secrets and configuration safely across environments, monitoring and alerting on production health, deploying with zero downtime, and the architectural judgment to keep a production system reliable as it evolves.

moduleGoal.primary: Extend Module 21's CI/CD pipeline into a complete build-and-deploy pipeline, and containerize a full stack application with Docker for genuinely consistent environments.
moduleGoal.secondary: Manage secrets and configuration safely across environments, monitor production health with real alerting, and deploy without downtime, applying this curriculum's full evidence-based discipline to production infrastructure itself.
moduleGoal.outcomeStatement: By the end of this module, you will be able to take a working application from a developer's own machine to a genuinely production-grade, continuously deployed, monitored, zero-downtime infrastructure — understanding precisely what each piece of that infrastructure guarantees, and why each one is genuinely necessary at real production scale.

lessons.title: CI/CD Pipelines
lessons.lessonGoal: Extend Module 21's test-only CI/CD pipeline into a complete build-and-deploy pipeline, understanding precisely what genuinely new stages a deployment pipeline adds beyond testing.

sections.title: Extending A Pipeline You've Already Built, Not Learning An Entirely New Concept
sections.content: Module 21, lesson 6 built a CI/CD pipeline that ran tests automatically and gated a deploy job behind their success — but that deploy job was left as a single placeholder line (echo "Deploying..."). This lesson fills in that exact placeholder with genuine substance: a complete deployment pipeline adds BUILD stages (compiling TypeScript, bundling a frontend, building lesson 2's Docker image) and genuine DEPLOY stages (pushing that build to actual hosting infrastructure) after the testing stages Module 21 already covered — the same fail-fast, sequenced philosophy, now extended with the actual, concrete work of getting tested code into production.

sections.title: A Factory Assembly Line Extended Past Its Final Quality-Control Checkpoint
sections.content: Module 21's pipeline was like a factory assembly line ending precisely at a quality-control checkpoint: every product that passes inspection sits there, confirmed good, but never actually leaves the factory to reach a real customer. This lesson extends that exact same assembly line PAST that checkpoint: a confirmed-good product now continues to a packaging stage (the build step, assembling the final, deployable artifact) and then to an actual shipping stage (the deploy step, genuinely delivering that package to where real customers can access it) — the quality-control checkpoint itself doesn't change at all; the assembly line simply now continues meaningfully beyond it, rather than stopping short of actually delivering anything.

sections.title: A Complete Pipeline With Build And Deploy Stages, Directly Extending Module 21's Test Job
sections.content:
Extending Module 21, lesson 6's exact pipeline configuration with genuine build and deploy stages:

name: Test, Build, and Deploy
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    # ... Module 21 lesson 6's exact test job, unchanged ...

  build:
    needs: test  # Module 21's exact fail-fast dependency - build
                   # never even starts if tests genuinely failed
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '20' }
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm run build  # compiles TypeScript, bundles the frontend
      - run: docker build -t my-app:${{ github.sha }} .  # lesson 2's
                                                             # Docker image
      - run: docker push my-registry/my-app:${{ github.sha }}

  deploy:
    needs: build  # only runs if BOTH test AND build genuinely succeeded
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh ${{ github.sha }}  # lesson 5's actual,
                                               # genuine deployment
                                               # mechanism

sections.title: Why needs: build (Not Just needs: test) Is What Genuinely Prevents Deploying A Broken Build
sections.content: This is the single most important structural addition this lesson makes to Module 21's original pipeline: the deploy job's dependency is now needs: build specifically, not merely needs: test — a genuinely important, precise distinction. A change could pass every single test (Module 21's entire test suite genuinely succeeding) while still FAILING to build correctly (a TypeScript compilation error in code the test suite never specifically exercised, a Docker build failure from a missing dependency) — if deploy depended only on test, this kind of build failure would never actually block deployment, since the test job's own success doesn't say anything about whether the application can genuinely be built and packaged at all. Chaining the dependency through BOTH stages (build needs: test, deploy needs: build) ensures every single stage's genuine success is required before the next one even begins, directly extending Module 21's fail-fast philosophy across this lesson's two genuinely new, additional stages.

sections.title: Tracing Two Genuinely Different Pipeline Runs Through This Lesson's Complete, Extended Structure
sections.content: This traces through two different pipeline runs, directly demonstrating why the build-stage dependency specifically matters, beyond what Module 21's test-only gating alone could catch:
sections.explanation: Pipeline Run A demonstrates precisely the gap this lesson's extended pipeline closes that Module 21's original, test-only pipeline could not: a change that's functionally correct according to every existing test can still genuinely fail to build, and only a dependency chain that EXPLICITLY includes the build stage (not just the test stage) catches this specific category of failure before it ever reaches the deploy stage. This is the same fail-fast principle Module 21 taught, now demonstrated as a chain of MULTIPLE sequential gates rather than just the original, single test gate.

sections.title: How Real Engineering Teams Structure Their Complete Build-And-Deploy Pipelines
sections.content: Real engineering teams structure their pipelines with exactly this multi-stage dependency chain — test, then build, then deploy, each genuinely gated on the previous stage's actual success — specifically because each stage catches a genuinely different category of problem (Module 21's tests catch functional regressions; this lesson's build stage catches compilation and packaging failures; lesson 5's deployment stage itself can still fail for infrastructure-specific reasons even after a perfectly successful build). Real teams specifically value this pipeline producing a genuinely deployable ARTIFACT (a built, tagged Docker image, in this lesson's example) as its own explicit, durable output, rather than treating 'tests passed' as sufficient evidence that a change is actually ready for production.

sections.title: Common Build-And-Deploy Pipeline Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Configuring the deploy job's dependency as needs: test rather than needs: build, missing this lesson's exact gap — a change passing every test while still genuinely failing to build would incorrectly proceed to deployment.

2. Building and deploying directly from a developer's own local machine, bypassing the pipeline's own, consistent build environment entirely, risking 'works on my machine' inconsistencies that a centralized, standardized pipeline build specifically eliminates.

3. Forgetting to tag built artifacts (Docker images, in this lesson's example) with a unique, traceable identifier (like the commit SHA, ${{ github.sha }}), making it genuinely difficult to know exactly which specific code version is actually running in production at any given moment.

4. Allowing the build stage to succeed despite genuine warnings or partial failures that don't technically halt the build process, missing real problems that a stricter, more thorough build configuration would have caught and failed on explicitly.

5. Never testing the pipeline's OWN correctness by deliberately introducing a genuine build failure and confirming deployment is correctly, completely blocked, rather than only ever observing successful pipeline runs and assuming the gating logic works as intended.

sections.title: Extending An Already-Correct Foundation, Rather Than Building An Entirely New System
sections.content: This lesson's approach — taking Module 21's already-correct, already-tested pipeline and extending it with two genuinely new stages, rather than building an entirely separate deployment system from scratch — is a direct, concrete instance of this curriculum's repeated 'recognize what's already correct and build deliberately on top of it' discipline, exactly Module 18's MVC extending Module 7's routes, Module 20's OAuth extending Module 9's session issuance. A developer who recognizes this lesson's build and deploy stages as a direct, incremental EXTENSION of Module 21's already-understood pipeline structure, rather than an entirely new, unrelated concept, internalizes this lesson's content considerably faster and more durably than one encountering CI/CD pipelines as if for the very first time.

sections.title: Diagnosing A Pipeline Failure By Identifying Exactly Which Stage Failed
sections.content: When a complete, multi-stage pipeline fails, the pipeline's own dashboard directly shows exactly WHICH stage failed (test, build, or deploy), immediately narrowing the genuine investigation to that specific stage's own logs and concerns, rather than needing to investigate the entire pipeline as one undifferentiated unit — directly extending Module 21, lesson 6's own diagnostic approach (which specific test failed) one level up, to this lesson's now-multi-stage structure. A build-stage failure points toward compilation or packaging issues specifically; a deploy-stage failure (lesson 5's eventual focus) points toward genuinely different, infrastructure-specific concerns, and correctly identifying WHICH stage failed is the essential first step before investigating either category.

checkpoints.question: Why does this lesson configure the deploy job's dependency as 'needs: build' specifically, rather than 'needs: test'?
options: There is no genuine difference between these two dependency configurations

A change could pass every test while still genuinely failing to build (a compilation error in code the tests don't directly exercise); depending on build specifically ensures this category of failure is also caught before deployment proceeds
needs: test is always sufficient and needs: build provides no additional protection
Build failures can never actually occur if all tests have already passed
checkpoints.explanation: A change can pass all tests while still failing to build, since tests may not exercise every code path; depending on build specifically catches this category of failure that test-only gating would miss.

checkpoints.question: A pipeline's test stage passes completely, but the build stage then fails due to a TypeScript compilation error in a file not covered by any existing test. With this lesson's correctly-configured dependency chain, what happens?
options: Deployment proceeds anyway, since the tests already passed
The deploy stage never runs at all, since its dependency on the build stage's success is not satisfied - this change is correctly, completely blocked from reaching production
Only the test results matter, and the build failure is ignored entirely
This combination of events is technically impossible
checkpoints.explanation: Since deploy depends specifically on build's success, a build failure correctly and completely blocks deployment, regardless of the test stage's own prior success.

checkpoints.question: What is this lesson's central argument about its relationship to Module 21's original CI/CD pipeline?
options: This lesson teaches an entirely new, unrelated pipeline concept with no connection to Module 21

This lesson extends Module 21's already-correct, already-tested pipeline structure with two genuinely new stages (build and deploy), applying the same fail-fast, sequenced dependency philosophy rather than building an entirely separate system from scratch
Module 21's pipeline must be discarded entirely before this lesson's content can be applied
This lesson and Module 21 cover identical content with no genuine extension
checkpoints.explanation: This lesson directly extends Module 21's already-correct pipeline structure with two new stages, applying the same fail-fast dependency philosophy rather than building an entirely separate, unrelated system.

codingChallenge.solutionExample:
name: Test, Build, and Deploy
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '20' }
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm test

  build:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4

The deploy job must depend on the build job specifically (needs: build), not the test job
The Docker image must be tagged using the commit SHA (${{ github.sha }}), not a generic or static tag
Each job must include the actual steps needed for its stage (build/push for build, the deploy script invocation for deploy)
hints: The dependency chain must be sequential: build needs test, and deploy needs build - not deploy needing test directly
Tagging with the commit SHA, exactly this lesson's example, makes it possible to trace exactly which code version is running at any time
This challenge directly tests whether you've internalized this lesson's central needs: build (not needs: test) distinction

lessons.title: Docker Basics
lessons.lessonGoal: Containerize a full stack application with Docker, understanding precisely what genuine problem containerization solves that running an application directly on a server does not.

sections.title: Solving 'Works On My Machine' By Packaging The Entire Environment Itself
sections.content: Every deployment this curriculum has discussed so far has implicitly assumed the deployment target (a server, a hosting platform) already has the correct runtime, the correct dependency versions, and the correct operating-system-level configuration an application genuinely needs to run — an assumption that's surprisingly often wrong, producing the genuinely common, frustrating 'it works on my machine' problem. Docker solves this directly: a CONTAINER packages an application together with its ENTIRE runtime environment (the exact Node.js version, exact system libraries, exact configuration) into one single, portable unit that runs identically regardless of where it's actually deployed — the deployment target no longer needs to have anything pre-installed at all beyond Docker itself.

sections.title: Shipping A Fully-Equipped, Self-Contained Kitchen, Not Just A Recipe
sections.content: Deploying an application without containerization is like sending someone a RECIPE and trusting their own kitchen already has the exact right oven, the exact right ingredients, and the exact right equipment the recipe assumes — if their kitchen genuinely differs in any meaningful way (a different oven temperature calibration, a missing specific ingredient), the recipe might not produce the same result, or might fail to work at all. A Docker container is like shipping a complete, fully self-contained, pre-equipped kitchen ALONG WITH the recipe — the exact right oven, the exact right ingredients, everything genuinely needed, all bundled together as one single unit — meaning the SAME recipe produces the SAME exact result regardless of whose physical location it's actually set up in, since the entire necessary environment travels along with the recipe itself, rather than being assumed to already exist at the destination.

sections.title: Writing A Dockerfile And Building/Running A Container
sections.content:
A Dockerfile, describing exactly how to build a complete container image:

FROM node:20-alpine          # the EXACT base runtime environment -
                                # Node.js 20, on a minimal Linux distribution

WORKDIR /app                  # all subsequent commands run from this
                                 # directory inside the container

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install --production  # install dependencies INSIDE the
                                 # container's own, isolated environment

COPY . .                      # copy the rest of the application code
RUN npm run build              # build the application, INSIDE the
                                 # container, using the exact Node.js
                                 # version this Dockerfile specifies

EXPOSE 3000                    # documents which port the application
                                 # listens on inside the container

CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]  # the command that actually runs when
                                 # a container is started from this image

Building and running this image directly:

docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 3000:3000 my-app  # maps port 3000 on YOUR machine to
                                   # port 3000 INSIDE the container

sections.title: Why FROM node:20-alpine Is What Actually Guarantees Environment Consistency, Not Just A Convention
sections.content: This is the single most important mechanical detail this lesson must make precise: FROM node:20-alpine specifies the EXACT base image — a complete, specific, versioned snapshot of an operating system with Node.js 20 already installed — that this container will genuinely be built on top of, regardless of WHERE the docker build command is actually run. This is precisely what eliminates the 'works on my machine' problem this lesson's definition described: a developer building this image on their own laptop and a CI/CD pipeline (lesson 1's exact build stage) building the SAME Dockerfile both produce a container running the EXACT same Node.js version, on the EXACT same base operating system, regardless of what's actually installed on either the developer's laptop or the pipeline's own build machine — the base image itself, not whatever happens to already exist on a given machine, is what genuinely determines the container's actual runtime environment.

sections.title: A Complete, Multi-Stage Dockerfile Optimizing For A Smaller, More Secure Final Image
sections.content: This builds a genuinely more production-appropriate Dockerfile, using a multi-stage build to keep the final, deployed image lean:
sections.code:
# STAGE 1 - build stage, with all the tools needed to build the
# application, but which will NOT be included in the final image
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install  # includes devDependencies, genuinely needed for
                   # the build step itself
COPY . .
RUN npm run build  # produces the compiled, ready-to-run output

# STAGE 2 - the actual, final production image, genuinely lean,
# containing ONLY what's needed to RUN the already-built application
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install --production  # only PRODUCTION dependencies, never
                                 # the build-time devDependencies
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist  # copy ONLY the already-built
                                         # output from stage 1 - none
                                         # of stage 1's build tools or
                                         # source code are included here

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
sections.explanation: This multi-stage build directly demonstrates a genuinely valuable production refinement: stage 1 (the 'builder' stage) includes everything genuinely needed to BUILD the application (full devDependencies, the complete source code), but NONE of that ever makes it into the FINAL image — stage 2 starts completely fresh from the same base image, installs ONLY production dependencies, and copies ONLY the already-compiled output (COPY --from=builder) from stage 1. This produces a genuinely smaller, more secure final image (no unnecessary build tools, no devDependencies, no raw source code sitting in the deployed container at all), directly extending Module 22's general 'don't include more than genuinely necessary' discipline to container image construction specifically.

sections.title: Why Real Production Teams Universally Containerize Their Deployments
sections.content: Real production engineering teams almost universally containerize their applications specifically because this lesson's 'works on my machine' problem is a genuinely common, costly, and entirely avoidable source of production incidents — a containerized application's behavior is guaranteed identical across a developer's laptop, a CI/CD pipeline's build environment, and the actual production servers, since all three are genuinely running the exact same container image, built from the exact same Dockerfile. Real teams specifically value multi-stage builds (this lesson's codeLesson pattern) for the genuine, measurable difference in final image size and security surface, particularly at the scale where many container images are built and deployed frequently, where unnecessary image bloat has real, accumulating storage and transfer cost implications.

sections.title: Common Docker Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Installing ALL dependencies (including devDependencies) in the FINAL, production image rather than using a multi-stage build, unnecessarily bloating the deployed container with build-time tools that serve no purpose once the application is actually built.

2. Forgetting to specify an exact, pinned base image version (using a generic, unpinned 'latest' tag instead of a specific version like node:20-alpine), risking the EXACT environment consistency this lesson's entire premise depends on, since 'latest' can silently point to a genuinely different image at different points in time.

3. Copying the entire application directory (including node_modules, .git, or other genuinely unnecessary directories) into the container without a .dockerignore file excluding them, unnecessarily bloating both the build context and the resulting image.

4. Forgetting EXPOSE or the correct port mapping when running a container, making an otherwise correctly-built application genuinely unreachable from outside the container despite running perfectly fine internally.

5. Assuming containerization alone solves every deployment concern, when genuine production readiness still requires this module's remaining lessons (environment-specific configuration, monitoring, zero-downtime deployment strategies) layered on top of a correctly-built container.

sections.title: Eliminating An Entire Category Of Environment-Dependent Bugs Through Genuine Environmental Determinism
sections.content: This lesson's core value — a container's behavior being genuinely, completely determined by its Dockerfile, rather than by whatever happens to already exist on a given deployment target — is a specific, concrete instance of this curriculum's repeated argument for converting fragile, assumption-dependent correctness into structural, guaranteed correctness (Module 9's middleware composition making authentication structurally unavoidable; Module 21's CI/CD pipeline making testing structurally mandatory). Docker makes ENVIRONMENTAL CONSISTENCY itself a structural, guaranteed property of a deployment, rather than a fragile assumption resting on hoping every deployment target happens to have the exact right tools already installed.

sections.title: Diagnosing A Container That Builds Successfully But Behaves Unexpectedly At Runtime
sections.content: If a container builds successfully but the running application behaves unexpectedly, directly running an interactive shell INSIDE the container (docker run -it my-app sh) to inspect its actual, internal filesystem and environment directly — confirming the expected files genuinely exist at the expected paths, confirming environment variables are genuinely set as intended (lesson 3's exact concern) — is the most direct, valuable diagnostic step, since it lets you observe the container's actual internal state directly, rather than only inferring it from the Dockerfile's own written instructions and assuming they executed exactly as intended.

checkpoints.question: What genuine problem does Docker containerization solve that running an application directly on a server, without containerization, does not?
options: Docker provides no genuine benefit over running an application directly on a server

Docker packages an application together with its entire runtime environment, eliminating the 'works on my machine' problem where a deployment target's actual installed environment might genuinely differ from what the application assumes it has available
Docker only works for frontend applications, never backend services
Docker eliminates the need for any code at all
checkpoints.explanation: Docker eliminates 'works on my machine' inconsistencies by packaging an application with its complete runtime environment, guaranteeing identical behavior regardless of what's actually installed on a given deployment target.

checkpoints.question: A Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build, with stage 1 installing all devDependencies and building the application, and stage 2 copying ONLY the compiled output and installing ONLY production dependencies. What genuine benefit does this provide over a single-stage build that includes everything?
options: There is no genuine benefit; both approaches produce identical results
The final image is genuinely smaller and more secure, since build-time tools, devDependencies, and raw source code never make it into the deployed container at all
Multi-stage builds always produce larger images than single-stage builds
Multi-stage builds are required by Docker and cannot technically be avoided
checkpoints.explanation: Multi-stage builds produce genuinely smaller, more secure final images by excluding build-time tools, devDependencies, and raw source code that aren't needed to actually run the already-built application.

checkpoints.question: Why does pinning a Dockerfile's base image to a specific version (node:20-alpine) rather than a generic 'latest' tag matter for this lesson's central environment-consistency guarantee?
options: Version pinning has no genuine effect on environment consistency

An unpinned 'latest' tag can silently point to a genuinely different image at different points in time, undermining the exact environmental consistency guarantee this lesson's entire premise depends on
'latest' always refers to the exact same image forever, making pinning unnecessary
Base image versions are purely cosmetic and have no relationship to actual container behavior
checkpoints.explanation: An unpinned 'latest' tag can point to different images over time, undermining the guarantee of exact environmental consistency that pinning to a specific version provides.

codingChallenge.title: Build A Complete, Multi-Stage Dockerfile For A Node.js API
codingChallenge.description: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a Node.js/Express API: a builder stage installing all dependencies and running a build script, and a final stage installing only production dependencies and copying only the built output, with a pinned base image version throughout.
codingChallenge.starterCode:
# TODO: STAGE 1 (builder) - pinned base image, install all
# dependencies, copy source, run build

# TODO: STAGE 2 (final) - pinned base image, install only production
# dependencies, copy ONLY the built output from stage 1, expose the
# correct port, set the correct CMD
codingChallenge.solutionExample:
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install --production
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist

EXPOSE 3000
